en: Points of Controversy,
Great Fifty,
Second Chapter
Regarding the Discourse on Designation:
Is the designation of the Buddha, the Blessed One, supramundane?
Yes, it is.

"Is it not the case that [the teaching] strikes against the supramundane ear and not the mundane one; that they understand with supramundane consciousness and not with mundane consciousness; and that the disciples understand and not the worldlings?
One should not say so... [etc. ...
Is it not true that the discourse of the Buddha, the Blessed One, strikes against the mundane ear?
“Yes.
[If you say] “Yes,” then surely it should not be said that “the speech of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is supramundane,” since his speech is obstructed by the worldly ear.
Is it not the case that they understand the discourse of the Buddha, the Blessed One, by means of mundane consciousness?
Yes, it is so.

If they indeed understand the discourse of the Buddha, the Blessed One, by means of mundane consciousness, then surely you should not say: [that they understand it by means of supramundane consciousness].
“The discourse of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is supramundane.
But do not ordinary worldlings understand the discourse of the Buddha, the Blessed One?
Yes, they do.
If ordinary persons understand the speech of the Buddha, the Blessed One, then indeed it should not be said that "the speech of the Buddha,
the Blessed One, is supramundane. Is the speech of the Buddha, the Blessed One, supramundane?
“Yes. The path, the fruit, and Nibbāna; the stream-entry path and the stream-entry fruit; the once-return path and the once-return fruit;
the non-return path and the non-return fruit; the arahant path and the arahant fruit; the foundations of mindfulness and the right efforts.
Is the basis of psychic power (iddhipāda), the faculty (indriya), the power (bala),
and the factor of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) supramundane (lokuttara)? One should not say so …pe… Is the terminology (vohāra) of the Buddha, the Blessed One, supramundane?
“Yes.
“Is there anyone who hears the conventional expression of the Buddha, the Blessed One?
“Yes.”
Is supramundane dhamma cognizable by the ear, does it strike upon the ear, and does it come within the range of the ear?
One should not say so… [as before]… Is it not the case that supramundane dhamma is not cognizable by the ear, does not strike upon the ear, and does not come within the range of the ear?
“Yes.
“If supramundane phenomena are not cognizable by the ear, do not strike the ear, and do not come within the range of the ear, then indeed, sir, you should not say:
‘The conventional usage of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is supramundane.’”
Is the terminology of the Buddha, the Blessed One, supramundane? Yes.
Are there any who would become attached to the terminology of the Buddha, the Blessed One?
“Yes,” you say.
“Is supramundane dhamma provocative of lust, exciting, desirable, intoxicating, binding, and deluding?
You must not say so … [and so on].
Is it not the case that the supramundane Dhamma is not a basis for lust, not provocative of passion, not desirable, not intoxicating, not binding, and not deluding?
Yes, it is.

Since the supramundane Dhamma is indeed not a basis for lust, not provocative of passion, not desirable, not intoxicating, not binding, and not deluding, then surely you should not say: [that the supramundane Dhamma is the cause of lust].
“The discourse of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is supramundane.
Is the discourse of the Buddha, the Blessed One, supramundane? Yes.
"Is it possible that some would find fault with the speech of the Buddha, the Blessed One?
"Yes.
"Is the supramundane Dhamma a basis for hatred, a basis for anger, and a basis for resentment?"
It should not be said so… [as before]… Is it not the case that supramundane dhamma is not provocative of hatred, not provocative of anger, and not provocative of resentment?
Yes, it is.
If supramundane phenomena (lokuttara-dhamma) are not occasions for hatred, not occasions for anger, and not occasions for resentment, then indeed it should not be said:
"The discourse of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is supramundane.
Is the discourse of the Buddha, the Blessed One, supramundane?
“Yes.
“Is it the case that some might be confused regarding the conventional terminology of the Buddha, the Blessed One?
“Yes.”
Is the supramundane state a basis for delusion, a cause of ignorance, a cause of lack of vision, a cessation of wisdom, on the side of affliction, and not conducive to Nibbāna?

One should not say so… [as before] … Is it not the case that the supramundane state is not a basis for delusion, not a cause of ignorance, not a cause of lack of vision, an increase of wisdom, not on the side of affliction, and conducive to Nibbāna?
“Yes.

“If supramundane phenomena are not a basis for delusion, do not cause ignorance, do not cause lack of vision, increase wisdom, belong to the side of non-affliction, and lead to Nibbāna, then indeed you should not say:
‘The conventional usage of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is supramundane.’”
Is the terminology of the Buddha, the Blessed One, supramundane? Yes.
Do all those who hear the terminology of the Buddha, the Blessed One, develop the path?
It should not be said thus… [as before]… Do all those who hear the conventional expression of the Buddha, the Blessed One, develop the Path?
Yes.
Do foolish worldlings hear the conventional expression of the Buddha, the Blessed One? Do foolish worldlings cultivate the path?
One should not say so...
[and so on] ...does a matricide cultivate the path? [One should not say so.]...
a patricide … a murderer of an arahant … one who sheds the blood [of a Tathāgata] …
Does a schismatic hear the terminology of the Buddha, the Blessed One, [thinking], "The schismatic is developing the Path"?
Certainly not; it should not be said so...
Is it possible for both a heap of grain and a heap of gold to be pointed out by means of a golden staff?
“Yes, that is so.
“In the same way, does the Blessed One, by means of supramundane terminology, express both mundane and supramundane phenomena?
“Is it possible to point out a heap of grain and a heap of gold using a staff made of elephant dung?”
“Yes, that is so.
“In the same way, does the Blessed One employ both mundane and supramundane Dhamma by means of mundane terminology?
“Is it the case that the terminology of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is mundane when he employs mundane terminology, and supramundane when he employs supramundane terminology?”
“Yes, it does.
When one speaks in worldly terms, it strikes against the worldly ear; when one speaks in supramundane terms, it strikes against the supramundane ear.
When one speaks in worldly terms, they understand by means of a worldly consciousness; when one speaks in supramundane terms, they understand by means of a supramundane consciousness.
“Is it the case that ordinary worldlings understand when one speaks in worldly terms, while disciples understand when one speaks in supramundane terms?
One should not say so… [as before]… It should not be said.
“Is it the case that the terminology of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is mundane when he employs mundane terminology, and supramundane when he employs supramundane terminology?”—
Yes, it is.
But does the Blessed One not employ both mundane and supramundane Dhamma in his terminology?
“Yes.
“If the Blessed One employs both mundane and supramundane dhammas in his discourse, then indeed it must be said:
‘When the Buddha, the Blessed One, employs a mundane discourse, it is mundane; when he employs a supramundane discourse, it is supramundane.’”
Is the terminology of the Buddha, the Blessed One, mundane when he employs mundane terminology, and supramundane when he employs supramundane terminology?
Yes. When he employs the Path, it is the Path; when he employs what is not the Path, it is not the Path; when he employs the Fruit...
If one speaks of a fruit, it becomes a fruit; if one speaks of what is not a fruit, it becomes what is not a fruit; if one speaks of Nibbāna, it becomes Nibbāna;
if one speaks of what is not Nibbāna, it becomes what is not Nibbāna; if one speaks of the conditioned, it becomes the conditioned;
if one speaks of the unconditioned, it becomes the unconditioned; if one speaks of form, it becomes form; if one speaks of the formless...
It is formless; when one designates feeling, there is feeling; when one designates non-feeling, there is non-feeling; when one designates perception, there is perception;
when one designates non-perception, there is non-perception; when one designates volitional formations, there are volitional formations;
when one designates non-volitional formations, there are non-volitional formations; when one designates consciousness, there is consciousness.
Is it that for one who speaks of "non-consciousness," there is non-consciousness?
One should certainly not say so... [etc.
...The Discussion on Designation is finished.
